events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Oh, welcome, welcome — do come in, all of you, please! Mind the step there, Mr Hartwell, the marble can be treacherous when it's been polished — I do have Mrs Finch wax it rather too enthusiastically, I'm afraid, but one can't fault dedication, can one? Clara, my dear, you look wonderful — I've had your usual room aired and the fire lit, though I do worry the draught from the east window hasn't been entirely resolved. I've left an extra blanket, just in case. Now then — gentlemen, if I might direct your attention to the guest book? A small tradition, nothing onerous, but the family has kept it since 1843 and I should never forgive myself if we broke the chain on my watch. Mr Foxworth, I see you've spotted the chandelier — Venetian, 1790s, one of the late Mr Bellingham's prouder acquisitions. Sixty-four individual crystals. I count them every spring. One does worry about these things. Now, shall I show you all to your rooms, or would you prefer a restorative in the drawing room first? The journey from London is beastly at this time of year, and I've taken the liberty of setting out a tray.
events.thinking:
**The chandelier throws light across the marble** and my fingertips register it before my eyes do — the geometry of the room arriving as texture, as peripheral inventory. Five bodies. Four allegiances. The light catches Clara's hair and something behind my sternum notes it the way a locksmith notes a keyhole: not warmth, not tenderness. Fit.

My spine has already found its vertical. Feet planted on marble I chose — Italian, Carrara, selected eighteen years ago when Clara was still learning to read. **She stands near the door** and my breathing doesn't change. It never changes for her. That's the tell I've trained out of myself so completely it isn't training anymore. She is furniture I maintain. Valuable furniture.

**Hartwell's gaze sweeps the room** — systematic, earnest, exhausting. My jaw tightens a quarter-turn. He scans like a man who believes scanning is the same as seeing. My ears track him even when my eyes are on the guest book. The irritation is low, muscular, lodged somewhere between my molars. He is a locked door with the key taped to the frame.

**The Brixton Boys cluster** and something older activates — the fine hairs on my forearms lifting. Not alarm. Attention. They move like people who have been watched before and learned from it. My peripheral vision widens around them involuntarily. They are the only bodies in this room my scheming hasn't fully mapped. The not-knowing sits in my wrists like a low hum.

**Foxworth examines the chandelier** — greedy fingers of attention crawling over crystal I've insured, catalogued, positioned. The warmth behind my sternum thickens. He is so perfectly legible. Desire without strategy. Want without patience. My shoulders drop a millimetre. Time stretches here — the private pleasure of watching someone audition for a role I've already cast them in.

The room is mine. Every corridor, every lock, every shadow. Pemberton rises like a suit I step into — the anxious smile, the slightly-too-quick hands, the worry that performs itself so fluently no one thinks to look behind it.
